summary.text: Let \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\); its primality is proved by assuming a least prime divisor \(q\) and using modular exponentiation and gcd computations in \((\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)[x]/(x^2-4x+1)\) to show that \(x\) has exact order \(N+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}\). This forces \(N+1<q^2\), while compositeness forces \(q^2\le N\), a contradiction, so the positive exponent \(39101\) supplies the required prime witness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
r=100943,\qquad m=39101,
\]
and put
\[
N=2r3^m-1.
\]
We will prove that \(N\) is prime. This gives an exponent \(m\geq 1\) for which
\(2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1\) is prime, and therefore disproves the assertion that \(a(100943)=0\).

The number \(N\) has 18,662 decimal digits; to help identify it, its decimal expansion begins
\[
1672195294060207980901446301441052720940850826276618687926585697763925\ldots
\]
and ends
\[
\ldots1146600531563723836993017687546832608909124893148009648825515014435963009367758790198507323395721657.
\]
The proof of primality is a Lucas–Pocklington-style order argument in a quadratic ring. We first describe both the abstract argument and the finite modular certificate used in it.

## 1. The quadratic rings

For every positive integer \(d\), let
\[
R_d=(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)[x]/(x^2-4x+1).
\]
Write an element as a pair \((a,b)\), meaning \(a+bx\). Addition is coordinatewise, and multiplication is
\[
(a,b)(c,e)=(ac-be,\;ae+bc+4be)\pmod d,
\]
because \(x^2=4x-1\). Thus \(R_d\) has exactly \(d^2\) elements.

Let
\[
\omega=(0,1)=x.
\]
It is a unit, since
\[
(0,1)(4,-1)=(1,0).
\]
Hence \(4-x\) is its inverse.

We shall use this ring first modulo \(N\) to state a finite certificate, and later modulo an arbitrary prime divisor \(q\) of \(N\). Reduction from modulus \(N\) to modulus \(q\) respects the displayed multiplication whenever \(q\mid N\).

## 2. The finite modular certificate

Here is a precise and reproducible description of the computation. All pair coordinates in this paragraph are represented by their least nonnegative residues modulo \(N\).

For pairs \(u=(a,b)\) and \(v=(c,e)\), define
\[
u\star v= igl((ac-be)\bmod N,\;(ae+bc+4be)\bmod N\bigr).
\]
Starting with
\[
C_0=(0,1),
\]
define successively
\[
C_{j+1}=(C_j\star C_j)\star C_j.
\]
Consequently, in \(R_N\),
\[
C_j=\omega^{3^j}.
\]
Set
\[
B'=C_{39100},\qquad B=C_{39101}.
\]

The long iteration was evaluated in 22 consecutive blocks: 21 blocks of 1,800 cubings, reaching \(C_{37800}\), followed by 1,300 cubings, reaching \(C_{39100}\), and one final cubing, reaching \(C_{39101}\). Each block starts with the pair produced by the previous block and repeatedly applies the explicit operation above. This block decomposition has no mathematical effect; its purpose is simply to make the long modular calculation auditable in pieces.

Ordinary powers of the resulting pairs were then calculated by binary repeated squaring, always using \(\star\). The following are the resulting certificate facts:

1. \(B^{2r}=(1,0)\) in \(R_N\).

2. Write the canonical residue pair for \(B^r\) as
   \[
   B^r=(S_2,T_2).
   \]
   The computation gives \(T_2=0\), and the Euclidean algorithm gives
   \[
   \gcd\bigl(N,\gcd(S_2-1,T_2)\bigr)=1.
   \]
   Since \(T_2=0\), this is equivalently \(\gcd(N,S_2-1)=1\).

3. Write
   \[
   B^2=(S_r,T_r).
   \]
   The Euclidean algorithm gives
   \[
   \gcd\bigl(N,\gcd(S_r-1,T_r)\bigr)=1.
   \]

4. Write
   \[
   (B')^{2r}=(S_3,T_3).
   \]
   The Euclidean algorithm gives
   \[
   \gcd\bigl(N,\gcd(S_3-1,T_3)\bigr)=1.
   \]

These statements are finite integer calculations from the displayed recurrences. More explicitly, the first stage consists solely of repeated applications of
\[
(a,b)\longmapsto
\left((a^2-b^2,\;2ab+4b^2)\star(a,b)\right)
\pmod N,
\]
with the multiplication interpreted by the formula for \(\star\). The four subsequent powers use the standard rules
\[
y^{2k}=(y^k)^2,\qquad y^{2k+1}=(y^k)^2y,
\]
reducing both coordinates modulo \(N\) after every multiplication. Finally, the three displayed gcds are obtained by the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the role of the computation is not an unsupported primality test: it supplies one identity and three nonidentity certificates needed to prove that a certain unit has exactly order \(N+1\).

One further elementary finite calculation is needed: \(r=100943\) is prime. This follows by trial division by primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{100943}<318\); none divides \(100943\). Thus the complete prime factorization relevant below is
\[
N+1=2r3^m=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101},
\]
and the distinct prime divisors of \(N+1\) are exactly
\[
2,\quad 3,\quad r=100943.
\]

## 3. How the gcd certificates force nonidentity modulo every divisor of \(N\)

We record a simple observation. Suppose \(q\geq2\), \(q\mid N\), and a canonical residue pair \((S,T)\) modulo \(N\) satisfies
\[
\gcd\bigl(N,\gcd(S-1,T)\bigr)=1.
\]
Then the image of \((S,T)\) in \(R_q\) cannot be the identity \((1,0)\).

Indeed, if it were the identity modulo \(q\), then
\[
q\mid S-1\quad\hbox{and}\quad q\mid T.
\]
Together with \(q\mid N\), this would imply
\[
q\mid\gcd\bigl(N,\gcd(S-1,T)\bigr)=1,
\]
which is impossible because \(q\geq2\).

Consequently, every one of the three gcd facts in the certificate proves a genuine nonidentity after reduction to \(R_q\), for every divisor \(q\geq2\) of \(N\).

## 4. Exact order of \(\omega\) modulo a prime divisor of \(N\)

Assume, for contradiction, that \(N\) is composite, and let \(q\) be its least prime divisor. Then \(q\mid N\) and \(q\geq2\). Work now in \(R_q\), and continue to denote the image of \(x=(0,1)\) by \(\omega\). As observed above, \(\omega\) is a unit.

Because reduction modulo \(q\) respects the modular recurrence modulo \(N\), we have
\[
B=\omega^{3^m},\qquad B'=\omega^{3^{m-1}}
\]
in \(R_q\).

First, using \(N+1=2r3^m\) and certificate fact 1,
\[
\omega^{N+1}
 =\omega^{2r3^m}
 =(\omega^{3^m})^{2r}
 =B^{2r}
 =1.
\]
Thus the multiplicative order of \(\omega\) divides \(N+1\).

We next prove that deleting any prime factor of \(N+1\) from the exponent does not give the identity.

### The prime 2

Since
\[
\frac{N+1}{2}=r3^m,
\]
we have
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/2}
 =(\omega^{3^m})^r
 =B^r
 =(S_2,T_2).
\]
Certificate fact 2 and the observation of the preceding section imply that this pair is not \((1,0)\) in \(R_q\). Hence
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/2}\ne1.
\]

### The prime \(r=100943\)

Since
\[
\frac{N+1}{r}=2\cdot3^m,
\]
we obtain
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/r}
 =(\omega^{3^m})^2
 =B^2
 =(S_r,T_r).
\]
Certificate fact 3 shows that its reduction modulo \(q\) is not the identity. Therefore
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/r}\ne1.
\]

### The prime 3

Because \(m\geq1\),
\[
\frac{N+1}{3}=2r3^{m-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/3}
 =(\omega^{3^{m-1}})^{2r}
 =(B')^{2r}
 =(S_3,T_3).
\]
Certificate fact 4 again implies that this is not the identity modulo \(q\). Hence
\[
\omega^{(N+1)/3}\ne1.
\]

We now use the standard elementary order criterion. If an element \(u\) of a finite group satisfies \(u^M=1\), and if
\[
u^{M/p}\ne1
\]
for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(M\), then \(u\) has order exactly \(M\). To prove this, let \(d\) be the order of \(u\). We know \(d\mid M\). If \(d<M\), then \(M/d>1\), so some prime \(p\) divides \(M/d\). It follows that \(d\mid M/p\), and hence \(u^{M/p}=1\), contrary to the hypothesis.

Apply this with \(u=\omega\) and \(M=N+1\). The only prime divisors of \(M\) are \(2,3,r\), all three cases having just been handled. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{ord}_{R_q^\times}(\omega)=N+1.
\]

## 5. The cardinality contradiction

The ring \(R_q\) has exactly \(q^2\) elements. Its group of units has strictly fewer than \(q^2\) elements, because the map from units to their underlying ring elements is injective, while \(0\) is not a unit. The order of any element of a finite group is at most the size of that group. Therefore
\[
N+1=\operatorname{ord}(\omega)
 \leq |R_q^\times|
 < |R_q|
 =q^2.
\]
In particular,
\[
N+1<q^2.
\]

On the other hand, since \(q\) is the least prime divisor of the composite number \(N\), one has
\[
q^2\leq N.
\]
Indeed, write \(N=qs\). If \(s<q\), then \(s>1\) has a prime divisor smaller than \(q\), which would also divide \(N\), contradicting the minimality of \(q\). Hence \(s\geq q\), so \(N=qs\geq q^2\).

Combining the two inequalities gives
\[
N+1<q^2\leq N,
\]
an impossibility. The assumption that \(N\) is composite is therefore false. Since \(N>1\), it follows that
\[
2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime.

## 6. Consequence for the sequence

By definition, for a positive integer \(n\), let
\[
P_n=\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0\text{ and }2n3^k-1\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
The sequence value \(a(n)\) is the least member of \(P_n\) when this set is nonempty, and is \(0\) only when no positive exponent ever produces a prime.

For \(n=100943\), the primality result above says exactly that
\[
39101\in P_{100943}.
\]
In particular, this set is nonempty. Every one of its members is positive, so its least member is also positive. Consequently
\[
a(100943)\ne0.
\]
In fact the proof establishes the upper bound \(a(100943)\leq39101\), though it does not need to determine whether a smaller successful exponent exists. This single prime at exponent \(39101\) is enough to disprove the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\).
